justification: Single verify run, no re-run needed: Lighthouse 97/100/100/100, 0 console errors, 0 warnings, 0 broken links, mobileOverflowPx 0; only the expected NEEDS_MARKUS failure. Judged fresh, the page is at the 8.5 bar and a little over. Hierarchy: eight specific h2s and one correctly nested h3, long headings balance on two lines. Rhythm: prose, program, output panel, figure and callout alternate throughout; the longest unbroken prose is about one and a half phone screens. All three SVGs fit 390 px without scrolling, labels are legible, and they are theme-correct in dark (red dots, green coins, accent cells, shaded free-slot area, green/red series in Figure 3 all keep contrast). Each figure is informative rather than decorative and each caption says what to notice; Figure 3's caption even explains the missing zero point on the log axis. Output panels are visually distinct, all fit 40 columns on a phone, and the wildcarded ones now read as separate columns. Callouts are restrained (one dotnet, one warning, one pitfall), four exercises of four different forms with collapsed solutions are spread through the page, and the nine-item sources list is tidy in both themes. Against the ranking pages it is clearly better designed: yourbasic.org is about 450 words with one pseudocode block and two pictures; the Cornell CS 3110 chapter is about 3,300 words with no figures, code or exercises on the page; Wikipedia has one figure, one Python snippet and no measured data. What keeps it from scoring higher is phone code: around fifteen lines across five programs still run past the roughly 40 visible characters, and several of those are the operative line of the program (the carry loop in Increment, the MultiPop loop, the tick subtraction, the firstDebt guard, the x1.5 lambda whose '/ 2' rounding the prose later discusses). The blocks scroll and fade correctly, so nothing is broken, and MDN/Real Python have the same behaviour, but the brief's phone lesson asks for these to be wrapped. The remaining items are nits.
